title: Changes that go back and changes that do not: what cooking does to food for ever

summary.text: Stir a spoon of flour into cold water, and by the next morning you can have dry flour again. Heat the same flour and water for a few minutes, and it becomes a paste. The paste never turns back into flour. Your child tests both glasses and then tries every way back. They toast squares of bread for different times, and find which part of toasting goes back and which does not. They learn that heat swells starch, unfolds protein and makes new brown substances. They also find that tearing and grinding do not go back, although nothing new is made.
summary.art: Two clear glasses side by side on a kitchen counter, one with a white layer settled under clear water and one filled with a smooth cloudy paste, with a spoon standing in the paste.

intro.hook: A lump of ghee melts in a hot pan. Take the pan off the stove, and the ghee sets again. Pour dosa batter on the same hot pan, and no amount of cooling brings the batter back. Why does one change go back and the other does not?
intro.text: Both changes used the same pan and the same heat. The ghee only changed from a solid to a liquid. It was ghee before, and it was ghee after. The batter became something new, with a new colour, a new smell and a new feel. In this unit you sort changes into three piles: back easily, back with work, and no way back. You test flour in cold water against flour in hot water. You toast a ladder of bread squares, and you try to bring them back.
intro.art: A black tawa on a gas stove with a pool of clear melted ghee on one half and a round golden dosa cooking on the other half.

outcomes: I can sort changes into three groups: back easily, back with work, and no way back. I can name the way back.
I can explain that in a reversible change the substance stays the same, as in melting, evaporating and dissolving.
I can explain that most irreversible changes make new substances, as in cooking, burning, rusting and souring.
I can explain what heat does to the starch and the protein in food.
I can explain why toast turns brown, and why the browning does not go back.
I can test whether a change is reversible by trying a way back, in a fair test.
I can explain why tearing, grinding and mixing do not go back by themselves, although no new substance is made.
I can say why people cook food, and where people use changes that go back and changes that do not.

terms.meaning: A change that can be undone, so that you have the same substance as before.
terms.example: Melted ghee sets again when it cools. It is ghee before and after.
terms.art: A spoon of clear melted ghee beside a spoon of pale set ghee, with a two-way arrow between them.

terms.meaning: A change that cannot be undone. You cannot get back what you started with.
terms.example: A dosa cannot be turned back into batter.
terms.art: A bowl of batter and a cooked dosa, with a one-way arrow from the batter to the dosa.

terms.meaning: One kind of matter, with its own name and its own way of behaving.
terms.example: Water, salt, sugar, iron and wax are five substances.
terms.art: Five small heaps and bowls in a row: water, salt, sugar, an iron nail and a lump of wax.

terms.meaning: Something a substance does or is like, which you can test.
terms.example: Salt tastes salty, dissolves in water and has white grains. These are three of its properties.
terms.art: A pinch of salt under a magnifying glass showing small white cubes.

terms.meaning: A change between solid, liquid and gas. The substance stays the same.
terms.example: Ice, water and steam are three states of one substance.
terms.art: An ice cube, a glass of water and a steaming kettle in a row, joined by two-way arrows.

terms.meaning: To spread through a liquid as particles too small to see.
terms.example: Sugar dissolves in water. The water tastes sweet, so the sugar is still there.
terms.art: A spoon tipping sugar into a glass of water, with the grains fading as they sink.

terms.meaning: To change from a liquid into a gas that mixes into the air.
terms.example: Water evaporates from a wet towel, and the towel dries.
terms.art: A wet towel on a clothes line with faint wavy lines rising from it.

terms.meaning: Two or more substances together, each one still itself.
terms.example: Rice and dal in one tin make a mixture. So does salt in water.
terms.art: A steel tin holding white rice grains and yellow dal mixed together.

terms.meaning: A change in shape, size or state, with no new substance made.
terms.example: Tearing paper is a physical change. Each piece is still paper.
terms.art: A sheet of paper torn into four pieces on a table.

terms.meaning: A change that makes one or more new substances.
terms.example: When wood burns, the wood and oxygen become ash, smoke and gases.
terms.art: A burning matchstick with a curl of smoke, and a small heap of ash beside it.

terms.meaning: The substance that plants store as food in grains, potatoes and roots. Rice, wheat and cornflour are mostly starch.
terms.example: A grain of rice is about three quarters starch.
terms.art: A grain of rice cut open, with a zoom circle showing tiny white packed grains inside.

terms.meaning: A substance made of very long chains, folded into exact shapes. Living bodies are built from proteins.
terms.example: Egg white, paneer and dal are rich in protein.
terms.art: A long thread folded into a neat small ball, beside an egg, a cube of paneer and a heap of dal.

terms.meaning: What starch does in hot water. The tiny starch grains swell, burst and thicken the water.
terms.example: Rice flour and water gelatinise into kanji when they are heated.
terms.art: Three drawings in a row of one starch grain: small and hard, swollen, and burst with threads spilling out.

terms.meaning: To make a protein chain lose its folded shape, by heat or acid. The chain itself stays whole.
terms.example: Heat denatures the proteins in egg white, and the egg white turns solid.
terms.art: A neat ball of thread on the left and the same thread opened out and tangled with others on the right.

terms.meaning: The chemical change that browns hot, dry food. Sugars and parts of proteins react and make new substances.
terms.example: The brown colour and smell of toast come from the Maillard reaction.
terms.art: A slice of white bread and a slice of brown toast, with small wavy lines of smell rising from the toast.

explanations.concept: Three piles: back easily, back with work, and no way back
explanations.definition: A reversible change can be undone, so that you have the starting substance again. An irreversible change cannot be undone.
explanations.description: Many reversible changes go back with almost no effort. Cool the melted ghee, and it sets. Unfold the paper boat, and it is a sheet again. Other reversible changes go back only with work, time or energy. Salt stirred into water is still salt, but to get it back you must evaporate all the water. Rice mixed with dal is still rice, but someone must pick the grains apart. So this unit uses three piles. The first is 'back easily'. The second is 'back with work'. The third is 'no way back', which holds the irreversible changes. For every change, ask two questions. Is it still the same substance? What exactly would I do to get back to the start? If you can name a way back and it works, the change is reversible.
examples: Back easily: ice melts, and the water freezes again in the freezer.
Back with work: salt dissolves in water, and comes back when the water evaporates.
No way back: batter cooks into a dosa.
explanations.art: Three steel plates in a row labelled Back easily, Back with work and No way back, holding a folded paper, a glass of salty water and a piece of toast.

explanations.concept: In a reversible change the substance stays the same
explanations.definition: In a reversible change, no new substance is made. The same particles are there before and after, and only their arrangement or their place changes.
explanations.description: A substance is made of tiny particles, far too small to see. When ice melts, the water particles stop holding fixed places and slide past each other. They are the same particles. When water evaporates, the particles leave one by one and mix into the air. When they meet a cold lid, they gather into drops again. When salt dissolves, its particles spread out among the water particles, and each one is still salt. That is why the water tastes salty. In all these changes you can test the substance afterwards, and it behaves as it did before. Going back often means giving back or taking away heat. Ice takes in heat to melt, and gives the same heat out again when it freezes.
examples: Candle wax melts near the flame and sets again lower down.
Steam from a cooker turns into drops of water on a cold lid.
Sea water dries in the salt pans of Thoothukudi, and salt is left.
explanations.art: A zoom circle showing the same round particles in three arrangements: packed in rows, sliding loosely, and far apart.

explanations.concept: Getting a substance back out of a mixture
explanations.definition: A mixture can be separated when its parts differ in some property, such as size, weight or whether they evaporate.
explanations.description: In Cold Stir, Hot Stir, raw flour is stirred into cold water in glass A. Within half an hour, most of the flour lies in a white layer at the bottom. The water is poured off, the layer is dried, and it is flour again. That is a way back. It worked because raw flour does not dissolve. Its grains only hang in the water for a while, and then sink. Each kind of mixture has its own way back. Sand in water settles. Salt in water does not settle, but water evaporates and salt does not. Iron pins in sawdust come out with a magnet. Rice and dal are picked apart by hand or with a sieve. Every one of these takes work or time. A mixture never separates by itself.
examples: Tea leaves are held back by a strainer, and the tea passes through.
Farmers winnow grain: the wind carries off the light husk, and the heavy grain falls.
Salt is got from sea water by letting the sun evaporate the water.
explanations.art: A hand slowly pouring clear water off a glass, with a white layer of flour staying at the bottom.

explanations.concept: Most irreversible changes make new substances
explanations.definition: A chemical change makes one or more new substances. The new substances have properties that the starting substances did not have.
explanations.description: When a matchstick burns, wood and oxygen from the air become ash, smoke and gases. Cooling the ash does not give back wood, because the wood is no longer there. When milk sours into curd, bacteria turn the milk sugar into an acid, and the acid sets the milk. When an iron gate rusts, iron joins with oxygen and water and becomes rust. Wet cement also changes in this way. Cement does not harden by drying. It reacts with the water and grows tiny crystals that lock the sand and stones together. Cement even hardens under water. All the atoms are still present after a chemical change. They are joined in new groups, and cooling or drying does not put them back in the old ones.
examples: A dosa has a brown colour and a smell that the batter never had.
Rust is brown and crumbly, and iron is grey and hard.
A footprint left in wet cement stays in the hard floor for good.
explanations.art: A child's footprint set in a grey cement floor, with a trowel lying beside it.

explanations.definition: To gelatinise is what starch does in hot water: the starch grains take in water, swell and burst.
explanations.description: Rice, wheat, corn and potatoes store their food as starch. Starch is packed into grains so small that hundreds would fit on a full stop. In cold water these grains stay hard and closed, and they sink. That is the white layer in glass A of Cold Stir, Hot Stir. Between about 55 and 80 degrees Celsius, depending on the starch, the grains let water in. They swell to many times their size. Long starch molecules spill out of them and tangle with each other, and the water turns thick. That is the paste in glass B. A swollen, burst grain cannot close up again. So when the paste is dried, it becomes a hard, glassy flake and never a powder. Cooking rice, rotis, idlis and potatoes is mostly this one change.
examples: Rice kanji is used to stiffen cotton saris, because cooked starch dries into a stiff film.
Vadam and sandige are cooked rice paste dried in the sun into hard chips.
A raw potato is hard, and a boiled potato is soft all the way through.
explanations.art: A zoom circle showing small hard starch grains on the left and big swollen, burst grains with tangled threads on the right.

explanations.definition: To denature a protein is to make its chain lose its folded shape. Heat and acid both do this.
explanations.description: A protein is a very long chain, folded into an exact shape. Raw egg white is about nine parts water and one part protein. Each folded protein floats separately, so the egg white is runny and clear. Heat makes the chains shake harder and harder. At about 62 degrees Celsius, some of the folds start to come open. The opened chains stick to each other, and they join into a net that holds the water still. The egg white turns solid and white. In Tangled Threads you model this with six balls of wool that are shaken into one clump. The chains are not broken. They are only unfolded and joined to each other. There are so many of them, tangled so closely, that cooling does not sort them out. Acid does the same to milk protein. That is how lemon juice turns hot milk into paneer.
examples: A clear raw egg white turns solid and white in a hot pan.
Lemon juice makes hot milk split into soft white curds and pale whey.
Dal turns soft, and its raw smell goes, when its proteins are changed by boiling.
explanations.art: A frying pan with an egg, the outer part of the white already solid and the part near the yolk still clear.

explanations.concept: Why toast is brown: the Maillard reaction
explanations.definition: The Maillard reaction is a chemical change between sugars and parts of proteins in hot, dry food. It makes brown substances and many new smells and tastes.
explanations.description: In The Toast Ladder, squares of bread sit on a hot tawa for different times. Two things happen to them. First, water leaves the bread as vapour, and the bread goes firm. This drying is reversible. A pale, dry square left overnight in a box of damp air goes soft again. Second, the dry surface gets hotter than about 140 degrees Celsius. Then the sugars and proteins in the bread react. They make hundreds of new substances. Some are brown, and some have the smell of toast. This is the Maillard reaction, which the French doctor Louis-Camille Maillard described in 1912. It does not go back. A brown square stays brown after cooling and after a night in damp air. Boiling water never gets hotter than 100 degrees Celsius. That is why boiled rice and steamed idlis stay white. Sugar heated alone, at about 160 to 170 degrees Celsius, breaks up and browns in a different reaction and becomes caramel.
examples: A dosa is brown on the tawa side and pale on the top side.
Roasted coffee beans, roasted peanuts and a roti's dark spots are all browned by the Maillard reaction.
A steamed idli stays white, because steam is not hot enough to brown it.
explanations.art: Five squares of bread in a row, from white to cream to golden to brown to nearly black.

explanations.concept: No new substance, and still no easy way back
explanations.definition: Some physical changes are irreversible. Tearing, breaking and grinding make no new substance, yet they cannot be undone.
explanations.description: A torn sheet of paper is still paper. Atta is still wheat. A broken glass is still glass. No new substance was made, yet nobody can join the pieces as they were. So 'irreversible' and 'chemical' are two separate ideas. Mixing is a special case. A drop of ink spreads through a glass of water in a few minutes. It never gathers into a drop again. The Slip Shuffle shows why. With 2 dotted and 2 blank slips, the slips come out sorted about 1 time in 3. With 3 and 3, it is 1 time in 10. With 5 and 5, it is 1 time in 126. The more pieces there are, the more mixed orders there are, and the sorted orders become a tiny share. A drop of ink has more particles than anyone could count. Their random moving almost always leads to one of the mixed orders. A mixture can be separated, but only with work, such as evaporating the water. The Austrian physicist Ludwig Boltzmann gave this explanation in the 1870s.
examples: Wheat ground into atta cannot be made into grains again.
A drop of ink spreads through water and does not gather again.
A shuffled pack of cards almost never comes back in order by more shuffling.
explanations.art: A glass of water with a drop of blue ink spreading in swirls, beside a second glass that is evenly pale blue.

explanations.definition: Cooking is heating food so that it changes for good. It makes food softer, safer and easier to digest.
explanations.description: Cooking is the oldest chemistry that people do. It does three useful things, and all three are irreversible. It softens food. Swollen starch and loosened fibres are easier to chew. It makes food safer. The heat denatures the proteins of most harmful microbes, and these microbes die. Raw rajma holds a protein that makes people ill, and about half an hour of hard boiling changes that protein for good. It also lets the body take in more of the food. In one careful study, people's bodies took in about 91 parts in 100 of the protein from cooked egg. From raw egg they took in only about 51 parts in 100. Cooking has a cost too. Heat destroys part of the vitamin C in vegetables, which is one reason to eat some fruit and salad raw. Cooks use reversible changes as well. They melt ghee, dissolve salt and boil off water.
examples: Raw rice is too hard to chew, and cooked rice is soft.
Milk is boiled in most Indian homes to kill microbes before it is drunk.
Lemon juice is squeezed on food after cooking, so that its vitamin C is not destroyed by heat.
explanations.art: A kitchen counter with raw rice, raw rajma and an egg on one side, and cooked rice, rajma curry and a boiled egg on the other.

explanations.concept: Both kinds of change in living bodies, on the Earth and in the stars
explanations.definition: Reversible changes let the same substance be used again and again. Irreversible changes happen once.
explanations.description: Your blood carries oxygen by a reversible change. A protein in red blood cells holds oxygen in the lungs and lets it go in the muscles. Each red blood cell makes this round trip about once a minute. Growing is different. A sprouted seed cannot go back to being a seed, and your body will not be a baby's body again. The Earth also runs on both kinds. The same water has been cloud, rain, river and sea many times, because evaporating and condensing leave water unchanged. Rock melts deep underground and sets again as new rock. People copy these cycles. Glass, steel and aluminium can be melted and shaped again and again, which is why they are worth collecting. A phone battery holds a chemical change that charging pushes backwards. The Sun runs on a change that goes one way. Every second it joins hydrogen into helium, and it cannot turn the helium back.
examples: Water goes round as vapour, cloud, rain and river without being used up.
A steel tumbler can be melted down and made into a new one.
A chana seed who has grown a root cannot draw the root back in.
explanations.art: A circle of arrows joining a cloud, rain, a river and the sea, and beside it a single straight arrow from a seed to a seedling.

explanations.concept: Can an irreversible change ever be undone?
explanations.definition: Scientists agree that a cooked egg does not uncook itself. They disagree about whether 'irreversible' means 'impossible' or only 'far too hard'.
explanations.description: In the kitchen, 'no way back' is a safe rule. In laboratories the line is less sharp. Around 1960 the American scientist Christian Anfinsen unfolded a protein with chemicals, and it stopped working. When he took the chemicals away, the chains folded back by themselves and worked again. In 2015 a team in California and Australia took egg white that had been boiled for 20 minutes. They made it liquid with a chemical and spun it very fast in a thin tube. One kind of protein in it folded back into its working shape. They did not make a raw egg.
examples: A protein unfolded gently with chemicals can fold back by itself.
A battery's chemical change is pushed backwards by charging.
Nobody has turned a dosa back into batter.

perspectives.explanation: No atom is lost in any change. So with enough energy and the right tools, any substance could in principle be made again. 'Irreversible' describes what we can do today.

You can undo a change in one place, but only by spending energy. Spending that energy makes more disorder somewhere else. So the world as a whole never goes back to how it was. This is called the second law of thermodynamics.
For anyone who makes things, the difference is real and sharp. You can melt the ghee again, but you cannot take back the toast. Good work means knowing which step is which before you take it.

explanations.art: A boiled egg cut in half on one side, and on the other side a thin glass tube spinning in a laboratory stand.

agreed.text: Melting, freezing, evaporating, condensing and dissolving do not change what a substance is.
agreed.evidence: The substance can be got back and tested. Water from melted ice freezes at the same temperature as before. Salt from dried salt water tastes and looks like salt.

agreed.text: Cooking makes changes that do not go back, because heat changes the starch and the proteins in food.
agreed.evidence: Under a microscope, raw starch grains are small and closed, and cooked ones are swollen and burst. Cooked egg white stays solid when it is cooled.

agreed.text: A denatured protein has lost its shape, and its chain is still whole.
agreed.evidence: The Chinese biochemist Hsien Wu proposed this in 1931. Around 1960 Christian Anfinsen unfolded a protein with chemicals and watched it fold back and work again.

agreed.text: Browning needs dry heat well above the temperature of boiling water.
agreed.evidence: Food boiled or steamed at 100 degrees Celsius stays pale. The same food browns on a tawa or in hot oil, where its surface gets much hotter.

agreed.text: No atoms are made or destroyed in any change, reversible or irreversible.
agreed.evidence: When chemists carry out a change in a sealed container, the weight before and after is the same. Antoine Lavoisier showed this in the 1770s and 1780s.

agreed.text: Mixed things do not sort themselves out again, because there are far more mixed-up ways to arrange the pieces than sorted ways.
agreed.evidence: Ludwig Boltzmann worked this out in the 1870s by counting arrangements. Anyone can check a small case with slips of paper, as in the Slip Shuffle.

challenging.claim: A physical change can always be undone.
challenging.who: Many school books say this in a short form.
challenging.for: Melting, freezing, dissolving and bending a wire all go back, and none makes a new substance.
challenging.against: Tearing paper, grinding wheat and breaking a glass make no new substance, and they do not go back. Whether a change goes back is a separate question from whether it is physical.

challenging.claim: A change that makes a new substance can never go back.
challenging.for: Burning, cooking and rusting make new substances and do not go back in daily life.
challenging.against: Charging a battery pushes its chemical change backwards. Blood picks up oxygen and lets it go again about once a minute. Some chemical changes go back and forth easily.

challenging.claim: Cooking destroys the protein in food.
challenging.who: A belief found in some diet advice.
challenging.for: A cooked egg white looks and feels nothing like a raw one, so something has clearly been changed.
challenging.against: Heat unfolds the chains and leaves them whole. In a study of 1998, people took in far more of the protein from cooked egg than from raw egg.

challenging.claim: Raw food is always healthier than cooked food.
challenging.for: Heat destroys part of the vitamin C in vegetables. Fresh fruit and salads keep it.
challenging.against: Cooking kills harmful microbes and changes the harmful protein in raw rajma. It lets the body take in more of the starch and protein. Most people stay healthiest with some raw food and some cooked food.

challenging.who: Most people who have watched a wet floor turn hard.
challenging.for: Wet cement is soft and dark, and hard cement is pale and dry.
challenging.against: Cement hardens by reacting with water, and it hardens even under water. Masons keep new concrete wet for days so that the reaction can finish. Dried mud softens again in rain, and set cement does not.

challenging.claim: Cooking is what made our ancestors human.
challenging.who: The scientist Richard Wrangham, in his book Catching Fire (2009).
challenging.for: Cooked food gives more energy for less chewing. About 1.8 million years ago our ancestors' teeth and guts became smaller and their brains larger.
challenging.against: The oldest widely accepted traces of fire used by our ancestors are about 1 million years old. They come from Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa. Many scientists think cooking began too late to explain the first of those changes.

big_questions.q: A boiled egg holds almost every atom the raw egg held. So what exactly has been lost?
big_questions.hint: Think about Tangled Threads. The six threads were all still there after the shaking.

big_questions.q: Tearing paper makes no new substance, yet it does not go back. What really makes a change irreversible?
big_questions.hint: Compare tearing with melting. In which one could the particles find their old places?

big_questions.q: In the Slip Shuffle, six slips sometimes came out sorted by chance. Could a drop of ink in water ever gather itself again?
big_questions.hint: Remember how fast the chance of a sorted row fell as slips were added. It went from 1 in 3 to 1 in 10 with only two more slips. A drop of ink has far more particles than that.

big_questions.q: Glass can be melted and made again without end. Is a glass bottle ever really used up?
big_questions.hint: Ask where the bottle goes when it is thrown away, and what would be needed to melt it.

big_questions.q: People have cooked for hundreds of thousands of years. Did cooking change only the food, or the cooks as well?
big_questions.hint: Cooked food needs less chewing and gives more energy.

big_questions.q: Coal and oil took millions of years to form, and burning them is a change with no way back. Who should decide how fast they are burnt?
big_questions.hint: Think about people who are not born yet, and about the other animals and plants who share the air.

story.title: The Blue Drop on the White Sari
story.note: Yazhini, Vasanthi Periyamma, Sundar and the sari are made up. Periyamma is a Tamil word for a mother's elder sister, and anna means elder brother. These things are real. Batik is made by drawing on cloth with melted wax and then dyeing the cloth in a cool dye bath. The wax keeps the dye off the cloth beneath it. At the end the wax is taken out with heat. The cloth is ironed between sheets of paper or boiled, and the wax can be used again. Many cotton dyes join chemically to the cotton fibre and do not wash out.
text: The sari had to be ready by six o'clock. At four, Yazhini ruined it twice in one minute.

It hung over the long table in Vasanthi Periyamma's shed, six metres of white cotton. Periyamma made batik. She drew on cloth with melted wax, and then she dipped the cloth in dye. Where the wax sat, the dye could not reach, so the cloth under the wax stayed white.

This sari was for a bride in Mylapore. It was to have a border of blue fish and a wide white middle. The border was finished. Each fish had been left bare, and the cloth between the fish was sealed under wax. The middle was still bare too. Periyamma would cover it with wax after her tea, and then the whole sari would go into the blue vat.
Sundar anna was nineteen, and he had been learning from Periyamma for a year. He was stirring the vat with a long stick. Yazhini, who was nine, was only supposed to carry the tea.

She carried it too fast. Her elbow caught the wax pen, a little brass cup on a wooden handle. It rolled, and a line of hot wax drops fell across three fish. Sundar jumped to catch it. His stick swung out of the vat, and one fat blue drop landed in the middle of the white cloth.
Nobody spoke. The wax drops turned from clear to cloudy as they cooled. The blue drop sank into the threads and spread to the size of a one-rupee coin.
"Three fish will have white spots," Sundar whispered. "And the white part has a blue one. We have to start again, and there is no time and no more cloth."
Periyamma was at the gate, paying the dye seller. They had perhaps five minutes.

Yazhini stared at the wax drops. They looked like something she had seen that morning. At breakfast, a spoon of ghee had dripped on her steel plate and set into pale, cloudy beads. Then Amma had put a hot dosa on top of them. When Yazhini lifted the dosa, the beads were gone. The ghee had turned runny and soaked into the dosa.
"Anna," she said. "Is wax like ghee? When it is hot it runs, and when it is cold it sits. Is that all that has happened to it?"

Sundar looked at her, and then at the iron that Periyamma used for finished cloth. He laid a sheet of old newspaper over the three fish and pressed the warm iron down. When he lifted the paper, it had three greasy spots. He pressed again with a fresh sheet, and then again, until the paper came up clean. On the cloth, the drops were gone.
"It went back," Yazhini said. "It only needed to be warm again."

"Now the blue," said Sundar. He put fresh newspaper over the blue spot and pressed the iron. The paper came up clean, and the spot had not changed. He dabbed it with a wet cloth. He rubbed it with soap. The cloth around it got wet, and the spot stayed as blue as before.
"Warm it more," said Yazhini.

"It is not sitting on the cloth, kanna," said a voice behind them. Periyamma had come in. She did not shout. She bent over the spot and looked at it for a long moment, the way she looked at a drawing she had not finished.

"Wax sits on top of the threads," she said. "I send it where I like, and heat calls it back. Dye joins the cotton. Once they have joined, I cannot part them. Why do you think I do all my drawing in wax, and dip in the dye last of all?"
"Because you can change your mind about wax," said Sundar.
"And about dye, never," said Periyamma. "So I do not waste time wishing a blue spot white. I ask what a blue spot can become."

She picked up the wax pen and filled it. Around the blue spot she drew a small, quick shape and left it bare: a body, a tail, a fin. The spot sat exactly where an eye would be. Then she covered the rest of the white middle with wax, as she had always meant to do.

The sari went into the vat at half past four. It came out blue wherever the cloth had been bare. Sundar boiled it in the big pot, and the wax melted off and floated to the top in a yellow skin. Periyamma skimmed that skin into a tin. She would use the same wax tomorrow.
At six, the bride's mother unfolded the sari across both arms. A row of blue fish swam along the border. Far out in the white middle, one small fish swam alone, with a dark blue eye.
"That one has left the others," the bride's mother said. "Did you plan it?"
Periyamma glanced at Yazhini. "It happened," she said, "and then we planned it."

That night Yazhini helped to scrape the cold wax out of the tin. It broke into yellow flakes in her hands. It had been melted and set more times than anyone had counted, and it was ready to be melted again.
story.epiphany: The wax had only melted and set, so warmth took it out again. The dye had joined the cotton, and nothing in the shed could take it out. Periyamma's craft depends on knowing which change goes back and which does not. She does the one that goes back first.
ask: Why could a warm iron take out the wax drops and not the blue drop?
Why is it safer to do the step that goes back first, and the step with no way back last?
Where at home is there a job with one step that goes back and one that does not?

games.title: The Way Back: a card game about undoing changes
games.context: This is a card game about 24 everyday changes. For each change you decide whether it goes back easily, goes back with work, or has no way back.

setup.art: Twenty-four small cards in a shuffled pile on a table, and three paper tokens in front of each player marked Back easily, Back with work and No way back.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards into a pile.

setup.art: One child reading a card aloud while another player slides one token forward, face down.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads the front. Everyone else puts down one token, face down.

setup.art: The tokens turned face up, and the reader showing the back of the card.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the tokens over. The reader reads the back.

printables.title: 24 change cards: a change on the front, its pile and its reason on the back

items.f: Water turns to ice in the freezer.
items.b: Back easily. Warm the ice and it melts. It is water before and after.

items.f: Candle wax melts and runs down the side of the candle.
items.b: Back easily. The wax cools and sets. It is still wax.

items.f: Ghee turns hard and white on a cold morning.
items.b: Back easily. Warm it and it is a clear liquid again.

items.f: A wet towel dries on the clothes line.
items.b: Back easily. Wet it again. The water went into the air as vapour.

items.f: Steam from a pressure cooker turns to drops on a cold lid.
items.b: Back easily. Heat the drops and they become vapour again. It is all water.

items.f: A sheet of paper is folded into a boat.
items.b: Back easily. Unfold it. The creases stay, and it is the same paper.

items.f: Salt is stirred into water until it cannot be seen.
items.b: Back with work. Let the water evaporate, and the salt is left behind.

items.f: Sand is stirred into a bucket of water.
items.b: Back with work. Let the sand settle and pour off the water, or strain it through a cloth.

items.f: Rice and moong dal get mixed in one tin.
items.b: Back with work. Pick them apart, or use a sieve with holes of the right size.

items.f: Iron pins fall into a box of sawdust.
items.b: Back with work. A magnet lifts the pins out and leaves the sawdust.

items.f: Steel from an old ship is melted and made into new rods.
items.b: Back with work. Steel can be melted and shaped again and again, but it needs a furnace.

items.f: A phone battery runs down during the day.
items.b: Back with work. Charging pushes the chemical change in the battery backwards.

items.f: Dosa batter cooks on a hot tawa.
items.b: No way back. Heat changed the starch and the protein, and browning made new substances.

items.f: An egg is boiled for ten minutes.
items.b: No way back in a kitchen. Heat unfolded the proteins, and they joined into a solid net.

items.f: A slice of bread is toasted brown.
items.b: No way back. The Maillard reaction made new brown substances with a new smell.

items.f: Milk turns to curd overnight.
items.b: No way back. Bacteria turned milk sugar into acid, and the acid set the milk.

items.f: A matchstick burns.
items.b: No way back. The wood and oxygen became ash, smoke and gases.

items.f: An iron gate rusts in the monsoon.
items.b: No way back at home. Iron joined with oxygen and water and made rust, a new substance.

items.f: Wet cement sets into a hard floor.
items.b: No way back. The cement reacted with the water. It did not only dry.

items.f: A sheet of paper is torn into small pieces.
items.b: No way back, though no new substance is made. The torn fibres cannot be joined as they were.

items.f: Wheat grains are ground into atta.
items.b: No way back, though it is still wheat. Nobody can join the powder into grains again.

items.f: A hard green mango ripens into a soft yellow one.
items.b: No way back. Inside the fruit, starch turned into sugar and new colours formed.

items.f: A chana seed grows a small white root.
items.b: No way back. The seedling built their root from the food stored in the seed.

items.f: Rice is puffed into pori in a pan of hot sand.
items.b: No way back. The water inside each grain turned to steam, and the starch cooked as it puffed.

printables.title: 3 pile tokens: Back easily, Back with work, No way back. Print one set for each player

rules: One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud. The reader keeps the back hidden.
Every other player puts one pile token face down. Then everyone turns the tokens over together.
The reader reads the back. Every player whose token matches the pile on the back scores 1 point.
A player who chose a 'back' pile scores 1 more point for naming the way back. A player who chose 'No way back' scores 1 more point for saying what changed.
With two players, swap the reader's role after every card. The reader does not guess on their own card.
Playing alone? Read a card, say the pile and the reason aloud, then turn the card over. Score yourself in the same way.
After all 24 cards, the player with the most points wins. If you play alone, your score out of 48 is your result.

flow.do: Cut out the 24 cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards into a pile. Give each player one set of three tokens.
flow.say: Each card describes a change. Your three tokens are three piles: back easily, back with work, and no way back.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards. Take three tokens.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Way Back. You set up the cards and the tokens.

flow.do: Play the first twelve cards. After each card, read the back aloud. Ask the question below after card six.
flow.say: The reader reads the front of a card aloud. Everyone chooses a token and puts it face down. Then we turn the tokens over together. The reader reads the back. Who scored a point?
flow.kid: Listen to the card. Pick a pile token. Turn it over. Check the back.

ask.q: How did you decide which pile the change belongs in?
good: I asked if it is still the same substance.
I tried to name what I would do to get back.
If something new was made, I chose no way back.

flow.parent: A useful question for a stuck child is: what exactly would you do to get back to the start? One child can play alone or with you. With three or four players, take turns as the reader.
flow.context: In this step of The Way Back you play the first twelve change cards.

flow.do: Play the last twelve cards the same way. Keep the score on a piece of paper.
flow.say: Twelve more cards. This time, also give the reason. Name the way back, or say what changed for good.
flow.kid: Play twelve more cards. Name the way back, or say what changed.
flow.context: In this step of The Way Back you play the last twelve cards and give a reason for each.

flow.do: Count the points. Then sort all 24 cards into three piles and look at the 'No way back' pile.
flow.say: Let us sort the cards into the three piles. Look at the 'No way back' pile. Which of these made a new substance? Which did not?
flow.kid: Sort the cards into three piles. Which changes made something new?

check.q: Which of these has no way back, although no new substance is made?
check.why: Atta is still wheat, but the powder cannot be joined into grains. Burning makes new substances. Melted wax sets again when it cools.

flow.context: This is the last step of The Way Back. You sort the change cards into three piles and compare them.

items.f: A hard slab of peanut brittle
items.b: BRITTLE, card 4 of 4. This is the end of the line.

items.b: PAPAD, card 1 of 4. The next step is mixing with water and salt, and rolling. It goes back with work: dried dough can be powdered again.

rules: You need the 20 cards and 5 coins. All players work as one team.
Spread the cards with the fronts up. Do not look at the backs during the game.
Players take turns. On your turn, pick up any one card and place it in a row for its food.
Each row must run from the first stage on the left to the finished food on the right. You may slide cards along to fit a new one in.
When all five rows are built, put one coin in each row. The coin goes between two cards, at the first step that has no way back.
Now turn the cards over. Score 1 point for each card in the right place, and 1 point for each coin in the right place.
The most you can score is 25. A team that scores 20 or more wins. Playing alone? Build all five rows yourself and try to beat 20.

flow.do: Cut out the 20 cards. Shuffle them and spread them out with the fronts up. Put 5 coins beside them.
flow.say: These cards show five foods being made. Each food has four stages. We will line them up in the order of making.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Spread them out, fronts up. Get five coins.
flow.context: This is the first step of Line Up the Kitchen. You spread out the 20 stage cards.

flow.do: Take turns to place the cards into five rows. Talk about each card as it goes down.
flow.say: Pick a card. Which food does it belong to? Does it come before or after the cards already in that row?
flow.kid: Pick a card. Find its food. Put it in the right place.
flow.parent: If your family has never made one of these foods, say so and guess together. The backs will settle it at the end.
flow.context: In this step of Line Up the Kitchen you build five rows of four cards, in the order of making.

flow.do: For each row, decide together which step is the first with no way back. Put a coin between those two cards.
flow.say: Look along each row. Some steps go back and some do not. Where is the first step that can never be undone?
flow.kid: Look at each row. Find the first step with no way back.

ask.q: Why did you put the coin there and not one step earlier?
good: The step before only heated or melted, and that goes back.
This is the first step that made something new.
Grinding cannot be undone, so the coin goes there.

flow.context: In this step of Line Up the Kitchen you mark the first step with no way back in each row.

flow.do: Turn all the cards over. Count 1 point for each card and each coin in the right place. Read the backs along each row.
flow.say: Let us turn the cards over and count. Which food has a step with no way back at the very start? Which has it only at the end?
flow.kid: Turn the cards over. Count your points. Read the backs.

check.q: A cook melts butter and then heats it into ghee. Up to which step can the cook still go back?
check.why: Melted butter sets again when it cools. Once strong heat has boiled off the water and browned the milk solids, it is ghee and stays ghee.

flow.parent: The coins belong after these cards: soaked rice and urad dal, hot milk, cream, sugar syrup and sun-dried papad.
flow.context: This is the last step of Line Up the Kitchen. You check the five rows against the backs of the cards.

experiments.title: Cold Stir, Hot Stir: can the flour come back?
experiments.question: One spoon of flour is stirred into cold water. Another spoon is stirred into water and heated for a few minutes. After both have stood for 30 minutes, will the flour settle out of each one? Can dry flour be got back from each?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will the flour settle to the bottom of the cold glass? Will it settle in the heated glass? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same flour in both glasses, one level tablespoon in each. Use the same amount of water, 150 millilitres in each. Use two glasses of the same size, and stand them side by side for the same time. Only one thing differs: the mix for glass B is heated for a few minutes, and the mix for glass A is not. Heating boils away a little water from B. That is a small second difference, so write it down.
results_table: Glass A, cold: what you see
Glass B, heated: what you see

materials.item: cornflour (the white starch powder used to thicken soup) or rice flour: 2 level tablespoons. Maida also works
clear glass tumblers of the same size, labelled A and B
drinking water: 150 millilitres for each glass, which is 10 tablespoons
a small steel pan and a spoon for stirring
a gas stove or an induction stove, used by the grown-up only
steel plates, labelled A and B, for drying
small katoris, for the last test
a ruler, a clock or phone timer, the results table and a pencil

experiments.safety: A grown-up does the heating and pours the hot paste. Hot starch paste sticks to skin and burns, so let the pan cool for two minutes before pouring.

schedule.what: Mix both glasses and heat the mix for glass B. Watch both for 30 minutes, then set the two plates to dry.
Test the two dried plates and say what the results show.

experiments.record: Draw a table with rows for 0, 10 and 30 minutes, and one more row for the dried plates. For each glass, write whether there is a layer at the bottom and how thick it is in millimetres. Write whether the liquid pours.
experiments.context: In this experiment you stir flour into cold water in one glass, and into heated water in another. You find out whether the flour settles in each glass, and whether dry flour can be got back.

setup.art: Two clear glass tumblers labelled A and B on a kitchen counter, with a bowl of white flour, a tablespoon and a jug of water.
setup.caption: 1. Glass A: stir 1 level tablespoon of flour into 150 millilitres of cold water.

setup.art: A grown-up stirring a small steel pan of white liquid on a stove, with the liquid just turning thick and glossy.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up heats the same mix in a pan, stirring, until it thickens. This goes into glass B.

setup.art: The two glasses side by side, glass A with a white layer under clearer water and glass B evenly cloudy, and a ruler held against glass A.
setup.caption: 3. Look at 10 and 30 minutes. Measure any layer at the bottom.

setup.art: A hand pouring the water off glass A into a sink, with the white layer staying behind.
setup.caption: 4. Pour the water off A. Spread the white layer on plate A. Spread a spoon of B's paste on plate B.

setup.art: Two steel plates the next morning, plate A with a dry white powder and plate B with a hard, clear, curled flake.
setup.caption: 5. When both plates are dry, rub each one. Is it flour again?

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
rows: White layer 4 mm thick, thinner water above
White layer 5 mm thick, water nearly clear
No layer. A soft jelly that hardly pours
Hard clear flake that peels off

flow.do: Show your child the flour and the water. Let them rub a pinch of flour between their fingers. Ask for the guess and the reason, and write both down.
flow.say: One spoon of flour goes into cold water. One spoon goes into water that we heat. After half an hour, will the flour settle in each glass? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Rub a pinch of flour. Will it settle in cold water? In heated water? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think it will, or will not, settle?
good: Flour is heavier than water, so it sinks.
Hot water might make it dissolve.
Heat might cook it, like rice.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Cornflour gives the clearest result, and rice flour or maida also work.
flow.context: This is the first step of Cold Stir, Hot Stir. You guess what flour will do in cold water and in heated water.

flow.do: Your child measures 150 millilitres of cold water into glass A. They add 1 level tablespoon of flour and stir 20 times. Note the time.
flow.say: Ten tablespoons of water, then one level tablespoon of flour. Stir twenty times. Now leave glass A alone and write down the time.
flow.kid: Put water in glass A. Add one spoon of flour. Stir twenty times.
flow.context: In this step of Cold Stir, Hot Stir you stir flour into cold water in glass A.

flow.do: Mix the same amounts in the pan. Heat on a low flame, stirring all the time, until the mix thickens and turns glossy. This usually takes 2 to 4 minutes. Cool for 2 minutes, then pour it into glass B.
flow.say: Now the same flour and water go into the pan. Watch closely and tell me the moment something changes.
flow.kid: A grown-up heats the same mix. Watch. Say when it changes.

check.q: Why does each glass get exactly one level tablespoon of flour?
options: So that only the heating differs
So that the flour is not wasted
So that glass B gets hot faster
check.why: In a fair test only one thing differs. Here it is the heating. If glass B had more flour, you could not tell whether the heat or the extra flour made it thick.

flow.parent: The change is sudden. The thin milky liquid turns thick and slightly see-through within a few seconds. Keep stirring so that it does not stick. Let your child watch from a safe distance.
flow.context: In this step of Cold Stir, Hot Stir a grown-up heats the same flour and water for glass B.

flow.do: When glass A has stood for 10 minutes, look at both glasses from the side. Measure any layer at the bottom with the ruler. Record what you see.
flow.say: Ten minutes have passed. Look from the side, without moving the glasses. What do you see at the bottom of each one?
flow.kid: Ten minutes have passed. Look from the side. Is there a layer?
flow.wait: Wait until glass A has stood for 10 minutes
flow.context: In this step of Cold Stir, Hot Stir you look at both glasses after 10 minutes.

flow.do: When glass A has stood for 30 minutes, look and measure again. Then tilt each glass a little. Record whether each one pours.
flow.say: Thirty minutes now. Measure the layer again. Now tilt each glass gently. Which one moves like water?
flow.kid: Thirty minutes have passed. Measure again. Tilt each glass gently.
flow.wait: Wait until glass A has stood for 30 minutes
flow.parent: Use the waiting time for the term cards or the story. Glass A should show a white layer under thinner water. With rice flour or maida the water above stays a little milky.
flow.context: In this step of Cold Stir, Hot Stir you look at both glasses after 30 minutes and tilt them.

flow.do: Pour the water off glass A slowly into the sink. Scrape the white layer on to plate A and spread it thin. Spread 1 tablespoon of the paste from glass B on plate B, as thin as you can. Leave both plates under a fan.
flow.say: Now we try the way back. We take away the water and see what is left. What do you think each plate will hold when it is dry?
flow.kid: Pour the water off A. Spread each one thin. What will be left?
flow.parent: Spread both as thin as a coin, or they will take more than a day to dry. A sunny windowsill is faster than a fan. Keep the rest of the paste from glass B in a closed box in the fridge. It is a real glue, and The Tell-Tale Seal can use it.
flow.context: In this step of Cold Stir, Hot Stir you take the water away to see whether flour comes back.

flow.do: When both plates are fully dry, rub each one with a finger. Stir a pinch from each plate into a little water in two katoris. Then ask the three questions in your words to say.
flow.say: Rub plate A. Now try plate B. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.kid: Rub each plate. Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why.
flow.wait: Leave both plates until they are fully dry, by the next morning

ask.q: Which glass gave the flour back, and how do you know it is flour?
good: Glass A. It is a white powder again.
In water it turns cloudy and settles, like the flour at the start.

ask.q: Glass B was cool again by the time you tested it. Why did it not turn back?
good: The heat changed the flour into something new.
It was cooked.
Cooling does not undo what the heat did.

flow.parent: Plate A usually holds a white powder. In water it clouds and settles, as fresh flour does. Plate B holds a hard, clear or whitish flake. In water the flake stays a flake and slowly goes soft. The reason is that flour is mostly starch, packed in tiny hard grains. In cold water the grains stay closed, and they sink. In hot water they take in water, swell and burst. Long starch molecules spill out and tangle, and the water turns thick. A burst grain cannot close again. So the cold stir was reversible, and the hot stir was not.
flow.think: Cotton saris are stiffened with cooked starch. Why would raw flour in cold water not work?
flow.context: This is the last step of Cold Stir, Hot Stir. You test the two dried plates and say what your results show.

experiments.title: The Toast Ladder: can toast go back to bread?
experiments.question: Squares of bread sit on a hot tawa for 0, 1, 2, 4 and 6 minutes. Can cooling, or a night in damp air, turn any square back into soft white bread? Can a pale square still be made darker?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which squares, if any, will go back to soft white bread after a night in damp air? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Cut all the squares from the same loaf, and make them the same size. Use the same tawa on the same low flame. Turn every square over once each minute, so that both sides are heated. Keep one square off the tawa, to compare the others with. Only one thing differs between the squares: the number of minutes on the tawa.

Colour score and feel, after a night in damp air

materials.item: slices of plain white bread from the same loaf. Each slice is cut into 4 squares
a tawa or a flat pan, and a stove, used by the grown-up only
a flat turner, such as a dosa turner
a steel plate, with paper labels marked 0, 1, 1, 2, 4 and 6
a steel box with a lid, big enough for five squares
a small katori holding a piece of cloth wetted with 2 teaspoons of water
a phone timer, the results table and a pencil

experiments.safety: A grown-up does all the toasting. The tawa stays hot for several minutes after the flame is off. Do not eat the squares that spent the night in the damp box.

schedule.what: Toast the squares and score them. Send one pale square back to the tawa, and shut the rest in the damp box.
Score the squares again and say what the results show.

experiments.record: Draw a table with five rows, for 0, 1, 2, 4 and 6 minutes. Give each square a colour score: 0 for white, 1 for cream, 2 for golden, 3 for brown and 4 for dark brown or black. Write its feel too: soft, firm or crisp. Fill in the table twice: straight after toasting, and after the night in damp air.
experiments.context: In this experiment a grown-up toasts squares of bread for different times. You then try to bring them back to soft white bread, by cooling and by damp air.
