flow.do: Cut two slices of bread into 8 squares. Lay out the six labels. Ask for the guess and the reason, and write both down.
flow.say: Five squares will be toasted for different times. Then we will try to turn them back into soft white bread. Which ones will go back? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Cut the bread into squares. Which toasted squares will go back? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that one will, or will not, go back?
good: The pale one is only dried, so water might soften it.
The brown one is cooked, and cooking does not go back.
Once it is toast it stays toast.

flow.parent: Two squares are spare. Do not correct the guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Toast Ladder. You guess which toasted squares can go back to soft white bread.

flow.do: Heat the tawa on a low flame for 1 minute. Put five squares on it and start the timer. Turn every square once each minute. Take two squares off at 1 minute, and one each at 2, 4 and 6 minutes.
flow.say: You are the timekeeper. Call out one minute, two minutes, four minutes and six minutes. Sniff each square as it comes off the tawa.
flow.kid: Call out the times. Sniff each square as it comes off.
flow.parent: The square marked 0 never touches the tawa. If the 2-minute square is already dark brown, the flame is too high. Lower it and start again with the spare squares and fresh bread.
flow.context: In this step of The Toast Ladder a grown-up toasts five squares of bread for different times.

flow.do: Put each square on its label. Your child gives each one a colour score from 0 to 4, presses it with a finger, and records both.
flow.say: Score each colour: 0 is white and 4 is nearly black. Now press each one. Is it soft, firm or crisp? What did you smell?
flow.kid: Score each colour from 0 to 4. Press each square. Write it down.

check.q: Why is one square of bread kept off the tawa?
options: To compare the toasted squares with it
To keep the tawa from being too full
check.why: You can only tell how much a square has changed by putting it beside one that was never heated. The square marked 0 shows what 'going back' would have to look like.

flow.context: In this step of The Toast Ladder you score the colour and the feel of each square, straight after toasting.

flow.do: Let the squares cool for 3 minutes and look again. Then put one of the two 1-minute squares back on the tawa for 3 more minutes, turning it each minute. Compare it with the 4-minute square.
flow.say: The squares are cool now. Has any colour gone back? Now watch this pale square go back on the tawa. Can it catch up with the brown one?
flow.kid: The squares are cool. Did any colour go back? Can a pale square get darker?
flow.parent: Cooling changes no colours. The pale square, toasted for 3 more minutes, reaches about the same brown as the 4-minute square. So any square can still go darker.
flow.context: In this step of The Toast Ladder you check the cooled squares, and a grown-up toasts one pale square again.

flow.do: Put the 0, 1, 2, 4 and 6 minute squares in the steel box, in order. Stand the katori with the wet cloth beside them, not touching. Close the lid and leave the box overnight.
flow.say: Toasting drove water out of the bread. So tonight we give the squares damp air. Tomorrow we see which ones went back.
flow.kid: Put five squares in the box with the wet cloth. Close the lid.
flow.context: In this step of The Toast Ladder you shut the squares in a box of damp air for the night.

flow.do: Open the box. Your child scores the colour of each square again, presses each one, and records both. Then ask the three questions in your words to say.
flow.say: Score the colours again and press each square. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.kid: Score and press each square again. Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.

ask.q: What went back, and what did not?
good: The softness came back in the pale squares.
No colour went back.
The brown squares still smell of toast.

ask.q: Yesterday, could every square still be made darker? Could any be made paler?
good: Yes, the pale one caught up with the brown one.
No square got paler, whatever we did.

flow.parent: In most homes the pale squares are soft again, and the brown ones are bendy. Every colour score is the same as yesterday. The reason is that two changes happened on the tawa. Water left the bread, and damp air gave it back. That change is reversible. On the hot, dry surface, sugars and proteins also reacted and made new brown substances. That is the Maillard reaction, and it has no way back. Throw the squares away afterwards.
flow.think: Boiled rice never turns brown, however long it boils. Why not?
flow.context: This is the last step of The Toast Ladder. You score the squares after a night in damp air and say what your results show.

activities.title: Five Changes, Three Piles: which ones can you put back?

materials.item: squares of scrap paper, about as wide as your hand
a steel tumbler half full of water, and half a teaspoon of salt
a tablespoon of rice and a tablespoon of any whole dal or rajma, with a small plate
2 tablespoons of milk in a small katori, and 1 teaspoon of lemon or lime juice
three paper labels: Back easily, Back with work, No way back

schedule.what: Make five quick changes and sort them into three piles.

activities.record: Write the five changes in a list. Beside each one write its pile, and the way back if there is one.
activities.context: In this activity you make five quick changes at the kitchen table, with no heat. Then you try to put each one back, and sort the changes into three piles.

setup.art: A kitchen table with two paper squares, a tumbler of water with a spoon of salt, a plate of rice and dal, and a small katori of milk beside half a lemon.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the paper, the salt and water, the rice and dal, and the milk and lemon juice.

setup.art: A child's hands folding one paper square, with a torn paper square, a stirred tumbler and a plate of mixed rice and dal nearby.
setup.caption: 2. Fold one paper. Tear the other. Dissolve the salt. Mix the rice and dal. Add lemon juice to the milk.

setup.art: Three paper labels on the table with the folded paper, the tumbler, the plate, the torn paper and the katori of lumpy milk placed beside them.
setup.caption: 3. Try to put each one back. Then place it beside its label.

flow.do: Lay out the things and the three labels. Tell your child the five changes you will make. Ask which ones they will be able to put back.
flow.say: We will fold a paper, tear a paper, dissolve salt, mix rice with dal, and add lemon juice to milk. Which of these can you put back? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Five changes are coming. Which ones can you put back? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of Five Changes, Three Piles. You guess which of five changes can be put back.

flow.do: Your child makes each change, and then tries for a short while to undo it. For the milk, stir in the lemon juice and wait one minute.
flow.say: Make each change. Then try to get back to the start. Tell me exactly what you would do, even if it would take all day.
flow.kid: Make each change. Then try to undo it. Say how.
flow.parent: The paper unfolds at once. The rice and dal can be picked apart in a minute or two. The salt needs the water to evaporate, so pour a spoonful on a steel plate and look tomorrow. The torn paper and the lumpy milk do not go back. Cold milk makes small, fine lumps, and you see them best on the back of a spoon.
flow.context: In this step of Five Changes, Three Piles you make five changes and try to undo each one.

flow.do: Your child puts each changed thing beside one of the three labels. Talk about the questions below.
flow.say: Put each one beside its label. Look at the two things under 'No way back'. Is the torn paper still paper? Is the lumpy milk still milk?
flow.kid: Put each one by its label. Is torn paper still paper?

ask.q: The torn paper and the lumpy milk both have no way back. How are they different?
good: The paper is still paper, only in pieces.
The milk became something new: lumps and a thin liquid.
One is broken and one is changed.

flow.parent: This difference comes back through the whole unit. Some changes do not go back because a new substance was made. Others do not go back although nothing new was made.
flow.context: This is the last step of Five Changes, Three Piles. You sort the five changes and compare the two that did not go back.

activities.title: Tangled Threads: a model of a cooking egg

materials.item: pieces of wool or thick thread, each as long as your arm
a wide steel bowl

schedule.what: Model raw and cooked egg white with six threads, then try to go back.

activities.record: Draw the bowl twice: once with six neat balls, and once with the tangled clump. Label the drawings 'raw' and 'cooked'.
activities.context: In this activity six pieces of wool stand for six protein chains in egg white. You model what heat does to them, and then try to undo it.

setup.art: Six small neat balls of wool in different colours lying in a steel bowl.
setup.caption: 1. Wind each thread into its own small ball. These are folded proteins in raw egg white.

setup.art: Two hands shaking and stirring loosened wool threads together in the bowl.
setup.caption: 2. Loosen every ball. Shake and stir them together for 20 seconds. This is the heat.

setup.art: A hand lifting one thread and the whole tangled clump of wool rising with it.
setup.caption: 3. Lift one thread. Then try to get six neat balls back.

flow.do: Your child winds each thread round two fingers and tucks in the end, to make six small balls. Put the balls in the bowl and tilt the bowl from side to side.
flow.say: Each ball is one protein chain, folded up small. Tilt the bowl. The balls roll past each other, the way raw egg white flows.
flow.kid: Wind six small balls. Tilt the bowl. Do they roll past each other?
flow.context: This is the first step of Tangled Threads. You make six balls of wool that stand for folded proteins in raw egg white.

flow.do: Your child pulls each ball half open. Then they shake and stir all six together in the bowl for 20 seconds. Now lift one thread.
flow.say: Your shaking hands are the heat. Heat shakes the chains open, and open chains catch on each other. Lift one thread. What comes up with it?
flow.kid: Loosen the balls. Shake them together. Lift one thread. What happens?

check.q: In Tangled Threads, what do the six neat balls of wool stand for?
options: Folded proteins in raw egg white
Bubbles of air in an egg
check.why: Each ball is one long protein chain folded up small. Folded chains slide past each other, so raw egg white is runny. Once they open and tangle, they hold together as a solid.

flow.context: In this step of Tangled Threads you shake six loosened threads together, as heat shakes the proteins in an egg.

flow.do: Give your child two minutes to turn the clump back into six neat, separate balls. Then talk about the questions below.
flow.say: You have two minutes to get six neat balls back. Was any thread cut or lost? Then why is it so hard to go back?
flow.kid: Try to make six neat balls again. Was any thread cut?

ask.q: No thread was broken. So what changed?
good: The way they are arranged.
They are joined to each other now.
They lost their folded shape.

flow.parent: With six threads and nimble fingers, going back is slow but possible. One egg white holds many billions of billions of chains, and nobody has fingers that small. Around 1960 Christian Anfinsen found that some proteins fold back by themselves, if they are unfolded gently and kept apart.
flow.context: This is the last step of Tangled Threads. You try to undo the tangle and ask why it is hard.

activities.title: The Slip Shuffle: can shaking un-mix a mixture?

materials.item: slips of paper of the same size, about 2 centimetres wide. Three have a big dot and three are blank
a steel tumbler
a notebook page and a pencil for the tally

schedule.what: Shake and draw slips many times, and count how often they come out sorted.

activities.record: Make two tallies. In the first, count the sorted rows out of 12 tries with 4 slips. In the second, count the sorted rows out of 20 tries with 6 slips.
activities.context: In this activity you shake dotted and blank paper slips in a tumbler and lay them in a row. You count how often the row comes out sorted, to see why mixtures do not un-mix by themselves.

setup.art: Six small paper slips on a table, three with a large pencil dot and three blank, beside a steel tumbler.
setup.caption: 1. Make 3 dotted slips and 3 blank slips. Start with 2 of each in the tumbler.

setup.art: A child looking away while drawing a slip out of a tumbler, with two slips already laid in a row.
setup.caption: 2. Shake. Draw the slips out one by one without looking. Lay them in a row.

setup.art: A notebook page with two tallies, the first with four strokes out of twelve and the second with two strokes out of twenty.
setup.caption: 3. Is the row sorted, with all the dots at one end? Tally it. Then try with 3 of each.

flow.do: Make the six slips. Put 2 dotted and 2 blank slips in the tumbler. Explain that a row is 'sorted' when both dotted slips lie together at one end. Ask for a guess.
flow.say: We shake four slips and lay them in a row. A sorted row has both dots at one end. In 12 tries, how many rows will be sorted? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Shake four slips and lay them in a row. How often will they be sorted?
flow.context: This is the first step of The Slip Shuffle. You guess how often four shaken slips will come out sorted.

flow.do: Do 12 tries with the four slips. For each try, shake the tumbler, draw the slips without looking and lay them in a row. Tally the sorted rows.
flow.say: Shake, draw without looking, and lay them down. Dots together at one end? Then put a stroke in the tally.
flow.kid: Do 12 tries. Put a stroke for each sorted row.
flow.parent: Four slips can lie in 6 orders, and 2 of those are sorted. So about 4 tries in 12 come out sorted. Your count may be anything from 1 to 7.
flow.context: In this step of The Slip Shuffle you shake 4 slips 12 times and count the sorted rows.

flow.do: Add the third dotted slip and the third blank slip. Do 20 tries with all six slips. A sorted row now has all three dots at one end. Tally the sorted rows.
flow.say: Now there are six slips, and all three dots must lie together at one end. Will sorted rows come more often or less often than before?
flow.kid: Now use six slips. Do 20 tries. Count the sorted rows.
flow.parent: Six slips can lie in 20 orders, and still only 2 are sorted. So about 2 tries in 20 come out sorted. A count of 0 is quite common.
flow.context: In this step of The Slip Shuffle you shake 6 slips 20 times and count the sorted rows.

flow.do: Compare the two tallies. Tell your child the number for 5 dotted and 5 blank slips: 1 sorted row in 126 tries. Talk about the questions below.
flow.say: With four slips, about 1 row in 3 was sorted. With six slips, about 1 in 10. With ten slips it is 1 in 126. What happens to the chance of a sorted row as there are more pieces?
flow.kid: Compare your two tallies. What happens when there are more slips?

ask.q: A drop of ink in water has more particles than anyone could count. Will shaking ever sort them into a drop again?
good: No, there are far too many mixed orders.
It could happen, but the chance is too small to ever see.
Sorted orders are a tiny share of all the orders.

flow.parent: Mixing makes no new substance. It does not undo itself because the mixed orders vastly outnumber the sorted ones. To un-mix, someone must do work, such as picking, sieving or evaporating.
flow.context: This is the last step of The Slip Shuffle. You compare the tallies for four slips and six slips.

projects.title: Soak, Dry, Sprout: which change can a chana seed undo?

materials.item: dry whole chana, kabuli or kala, all of about the same size
a bowl of drinking water
steel plates
a clean cotton cloth, about the size of a handkerchief
a ruler, a notebook page and a pencil

schedule.what: In the evening, measure a row of 10 dry chana. Soak all 20 overnight.
In the morning, measure a row of 10 soaked chana. Put 10 to dry and keep 10 in a damp cloth.
Look at both groups. Keep the cloth damp.
Measure the dried group again. Look for roots in the damp group. Say what the results show.

projects.record: A table with three rows: 10 dry chana, 10 soaked chana, and 10 chana dried again. Write the length of each row in centimetres. Draw one chana from the damp cloth on day 4.
projects.context: In this four-day project you soak chana seeds, then dry half of them and let the other half sprout. You find out which change a seed can undo.

setup.art: Ten dry chana seeds touching in a straight row along a ruler, with the row ending near the 8 centimetre mark.
setup.caption: 1. Lay 10 dry chana in a row, touching. Measure the row. Soak all 20 overnight.

setup.art: Two steel plates, one with ten swollen chana spread out to dry and one with ten chana wrapped in a damp cotton cloth.
setup.caption: 2. Next morning, measure 10 soaked chana. Dry 10 on a plate. Keep 10 in a damp cloth.

setup.art: A row of ten slightly wrinkled chana along a ruler, and beside it an open cloth with chana who have small white roots.
setup.caption: 3. Two days later, measure the dried row again. Look for roots in the damp cloth.

flow.do: Day 1, in the evening. Your child lays 10 dry chana in a touching row along the ruler and records the length. Then all 20 chana go into the bowl, with water 3 centimetres above them.
flow.say: Measure a row of ten dry seeds. Tonight all twenty will soak. What will the row measure tomorrow? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Measure ten dry chana in a row. Soak all twenty overnight.
flow.parent: A row of 10 dry kabuli chana is usually 7 to 9 centimetres long.
flow.context: This is day 1 of Soak, Dry, Sprout. You measure a row of ten dry chana and put twenty to soak.

flow.do: Day 2, in the morning. Drain the water. Your child measures a row of 10 soaked chana. Spread 10 on a dry plate under a fan. Wrap the other 10 in the damp cloth on the second plate.
flow.say: Measure ten soaked seeds. Now ten will dry and ten will stay damp. Will the dry group shrink back to their old size? Will they still be alive?
flow.kid: Measure ten soaked chana. Dry ten. Keep ten damp. What will happen?
flow.wait: Do this the morning after soaking

ask.q: Soaking made the seeds bigger. Is that a change with a way back?
good: Maybe, if the water can leave again.
Yes, like a wet towel drying.
Not if the seed has started to grow.

flow.parent: The soaked row is usually about one and a half times as long as the dry row. Sprinkle the cloth with water morning and evening, so that it stays damp and not dripping.
flow.context: This is day 2 of Soak, Dry, Sprout. You measure the soaked chana, then dry half and keep half damp.

flow.do: Day 3. Look at both groups without measuring. Turn the drying chana over. Sprinkle the cloth with water.
flow.say: Look at both groups. What has changed since yesterday? Turn the drying seeds over, so that both sides dry.
flow.kid: Look at both groups. Turn the drying chana over. Wet the cloth.
flow.wait: Do this on the third day
flow.context: This is day 3 of Soak, Dry, Sprout. You look at the drying chana and the damp chana.

flow.do: Day 4. Your child measures the row of 10 dried chana and compares it with the first two rows. Then they open the cloth and look for roots. Ask the three questions in your words to say.
flow.say: Measure the dried row. Open the cloth and look. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.kid: Measure the dried row. Look for roots. Say what you thought, saw, and why.
flow.wait: Do this on the fourth day

ask.q: Which change did the seeds undo, and which change has no way back?
good: Swelling with water went back when the water left.
Growing a root does not go back.
The root is made from food stored in the seed, and that food is used up.

flow.parent: The dried seeds are usually close to their first size, with wrinkled skins. Most of the damp seeds have a white root 2 to 10 millimetres long. If no roots show, the room may be cool, so wait one more day. Soaking is a change the seeds can undo. Farmers use this. They soak seeds and dry them again, so that the seeds sprout faster after sowing. Sprouting is a change with no way back. Cook and eat the sprouts, or plant them. Soak the dried group again if you like, and see whether they sprout too.
flow.think: A dry seed can wait for years. What does a seed give up once they start to grow?
flow.context: This is day 4 of Soak, Dry, Sprout. You measure the dried chana again, look for roots, and say what your results show.

challenges.title: The Tell-Tale Seal: a letter that shows if it was opened
challenges.problem: Some things must show whether anyone has opened them. A medicine bottle has a ring that snaps. A jam jar has a lid button that pops up. Each of these uses a change with no way back. Your problem is this. Seal a paper letter so that nobody can open and close it without leaving a sign.
constraints: Use only paper, glue or flour paste, thread and a pencil.
The person the letter is for must be able to open it in 10 seconds.
The tester gets 3 minutes alone with the letter.
The tester may use fingers and a butter knife, and nothing else.
The maker then has 1 minute to say whether the letter was opened.
materials: glue, or the cooked flour paste from glass B of Cold Stir, Hot Stir
a piece of thread as long as your arm
a butter knife, for the tester
general: Glue the flap down along its whole edge, so that it tears when it is lifted.
Write your name across the edge of the flap, so that the letters break if the flap is moved.
Glue a thin strip of paper over the flap as a seal.
creative: Draw a pattern of fine pencil lines across the flap. After opening, the lines will not meet exactly.
Seal the flap with a strip of the thinnest paper you have, such as tissue. Thin paper tears before the glue lets go.
Lay a thread under the flap in a secret shape, and draw that shape in your notebook. Anyone who opens the letter will move the thread.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own seal. It must be easy for the right reader to open and impossible to close again without a sign. Draw your design. Test it three times with a different tester each time, and write how many times you caught the opening.
challenges.context: In this challenge you design a seal for a paper letter. The seal must use a change with no way back, so that it shows whether the letter was opened.

setup.art: A sheet of paper folded in three as a letter, with a glue pot, a piece of thread and a pencil beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Fold a paper into a letter. Seal it with glue or flour paste, paper, thread and pencil.

setup.art: A grown-up at a table carefully sliding a butter knife under the flap of a folded paper letter, while a child waits in the doorway with her back turned.
setup.caption: 2. The tester gets 3 minutes alone. They may open the letter and close it again, or leave it shut.

setup.art: A child holding the letter close to her eyes and pointing at a small tear beside the flap.
setup.caption: 3. The maker looks for a sign. Was it opened or not?

flow.do: Read the problem together. Look at a real seal at home, such as the ring on a water bottle cap. Ask how it shows that the bottle was opened.
flow.say: Look at this cap. Once the ring snaps, can anyone join it again? Which changes from this unit have no way back? Which could a seal use?
flow.kid: Look at a bottle cap ring. Which changes have no way back?

ask.q: Which changes with no way back could a paper seal use?
good: Tearing.
Glue or paste setting.
A pattern that cannot be lined up again.

flow.context: This is the first step of The Tell-Tale Seal. You look at a real seal and list changes with no way back.

flow.do: Your child folds a letter and builds a seal. Give the glue or paste 3 minutes to set.
flow.say: Build your seal. Remember that the right reader must open it in ten seconds. Which part of your seal can never be put back?
flow.kid: Build your seal. Which part of it has no way back?
flow.parent: Maida paste and cornflour paste both glue paper. A glue stick works too. Do not suggest improvements yet.
flow.context: In this step of The Tell-Tale Seal you fold a letter and build your seal.

flow.do: Your child leaves the room. The tester has 3 minutes. Toss a coin: for heads, open the letter and close it as neatly as you can. For tails, leave it shut. Then your child comes back and decides.
flow.say: I have had my three minutes. Look closely. Did I open your letter, or did I leave it shut? What sign tells you?
flow.kid: Look closely at your letter. Was it opened? What sign shows it?
flow.context: In this step of The Tell-Tale Seal a tester may open the letter in secret. You look for a sign.

flow.do: Talk about what gave the opening away, or what let it stay hidden. Your child changes one thing and says why it is better.
flow.say: What gave me away? If I fooled you, how did I do it? Change one thing in your seal and tell me why it helps.
flow.kid: What gave the tester away? Change one thing. Say why it helps.

ask.q: Why would a paper clip make a bad seal?
good: Clipping goes back easily, so it leaves no sign.
Anyone can take it off and put it on again.

flow.parent: The idea to draw out: a good seal uses a change with no way back. A paper clip or a rubber band uses a change that goes back easily, so it keeps no record.
flow.context: This is the last step of The Tell-Tale Seal. You improve your seal after the test.

items.p: What is a reversible change?
opts: A change that can be undone
A change that makes a new substance
A change that needs a stove
items.why: A reversible change can be undone, and you have the same substance again. A change that makes a new substance usually has no way back.

items.p: Which of these changes is irreversible?
items.why: Toasting makes new brown substances that stay. Melted ghee sets, ice melts and folded paper unfolds.

items.p: Salt stirred into water can be got back by letting the water ____.
items.why: The water goes into the air as vapour and the salt cannot, so the salt is left on the plate.

items.p: Melting changes candle wax into a new substance.
items.why: False. Melted wax is still wax. Its particles slide past each other, and they take fixed places again when the wax cools.

items.p: Match each change to its way back.
items.why: Each way back uses something the substance does. Ice melts when warm, wax sets when cool, water evaporates and salt does not, and a magnet attracts iron.

items.p: Sort these changes. Is each one reversible or irreversible?
items.why: Melting, drying and dissolving leave the same substance, so they go back. Boiling an egg, burning and cooking batter make changes that cooling does not undo.

items.p: Raw flour is stirred into cold water and left to stand. What happens?
opts: Most of it settles to the bottom
It turns into a thick paste
It dissolves and cannot be seen
items.why: Raw starch grains do not dissolve or swell in cold water. They hang in the water for a while and then sink. Flour turns to paste only when it is heated.

items.p: Cooked flour paste turns back into dry flour when it cools.
items.why: False. Heat made the starch grains swell and burst, and a burst grain cannot close again. Cooled paste stays paste.

items.p: Put these steps in order, to show how salt comes back from salty water.
items: Pour the salty water into a wide plate
Leave the plate in a warm, airy place
The water evaporates into the air
White salt is left on the plate
a: Pour the salty water into a wide plate
Leave the plate in a warm, airy place
The water evaporates into the air
White salt is left on the plate
items.why: The salt can only appear after the water has gone. A wide plate helps, because more of the water touches the air.

items.p: Heat makes the long protein chains in an egg unfold and ____ together.
items.why: The unfolded chains catch on each other and make a net that holds the water still. That is why a cooked egg white is solid.

items.p: Why does boiled rice never turn brown in the pot?
opts: Boiling water is not hot enough
Rice has nothing in it to brown
The lid keeps the light out
The water washes the brown away
items.why: Browning needs a dry surface hotter than about 140 degrees Celsius. Boiling water stays at 100 degrees Celsius. Rice does brown when it is roasted in a dry pan.

items.p: Wet cement becomes a hard floor. What kind of change is this?
opts: Irreversible: cement reacts with the water
items.why: Cement reacts with water and grows tiny crystals. Rain softens dried mud again, and rain does not soften set cement.

items.p: Explain in two sentences why melted ghee is still ghee.
items.a: Melting only changes ghee from a solid to a liquid. When it cools it sets again, and it looks, smells and tastes as it did before.
items.why: A strong answer says that no new substance was made, and gives the evidence: the ghee comes back when it cools.

items.p: A pale square of toast can be made darker. Can a dark square be made paler? Explain your answer.
items.a: No. The brown colour comes from new substances made by heat. Cooling, wetting or waiting does not turn them back into bread.
items.why: A strong answer says that browning makes new substances. It also says that a square can go darker and cannot go paler.

items.p: Draw raw egg white and cooked egg white as tiny threads. Show what heat changed.
items.a: Raw: several separate threads, each folded into its own small ball. Cooked: the same threads opened out and joined to each other in a net.
items.why: A strong drawing keeps the same number of threads in both pictures. Nothing is added or broken. Only the folding and the joining change.
items.art: Two empty circles side by side, labelled Raw and Cooked.

items.p: Tearing paper makes no new substance. Why does it still not go back?
opts: The torn fibres cannot be rejoined
The paper dissolves in the air
Torn paper is a new substance
items.why: Paper is a mat of tiny plant fibres. Tearing pulls them apart, and nothing puts each fibre back in its old place. The pieces are still paper.

items.p: A phone battery is charged. What does the charging do?
opts: Fills the battery with new metal
Melts the inside of the battery
items.why: Using the battery runs a chemical change one way. Charging uses electrical energy to run it the other way. This is a chemical change that goes back with work.

items.p: A careful cook adds salt a pinch at a time. Why?
opts: Extra salt cannot be taken out again
items.why: Salt dissolves into the whole dish, and no cook can pick it out. Too little salt can be fixed by adding more. Too much cannot be fixed.

items.p: Which pair shows one substance in two states?
items.why: Ice and steam are both water. Toast, curd and rust each hold new substances that the bread, the milk and the iron did not have.

items.p: Raw rajma can make people ill. Why is well-boiled rajma safe?
opts: Heat changes the harmful protein for good
items.why: Raw rajma holds a protein that upsets the gut. About half an hour of hard boiling denatures it, and it stays changed after the beans cool.

items.p: Every change that makes no new substance can be undone.
items.why: False. Tearing paper, grinding wheat and breaking a glass make no new substance, and none of them goes back.

items.p: The same water can evaporate and condense again and again.
items.why: True. Evaporating and condensing do not change what water is. The water in a cloud has been through this many times.

items.p: Sort these changes into three piles.
items.why: Wax and ice go back with a little warmth or cold. A mixture can be separated, but someone must do the work. Grinding and steaming cannot be undone.

items.p: Three of these changes make a new substance. Which is the odd one out?
items.why: Curd, rust and toast all hold new substances. Melted butter is still butter, and it sets again when it cools.

items.p: Six slips can lie in 20 orders, and 2 orders are sorted. About how many of 40 shakes are sorted?
items.why: 2 sorted orders in 20 is 1 in 10. 40 divided by 10 is 4. So about 4 shakes in 40 give a sorted row.

items.p: Put these steps in order, to show how ghee is made.
items: The cream is churned into butter
The melted butter is heated until it turns golden
a: The cream is churned into butter
The melted butter is heated until it turns golden
items.why: Melting the butter is the one step here that goes back easily. The strong heating at the end makes ghee, which never turns back into butter.

items.p: Some people think dissolved salt is gone for ever. What test would show that the salt is still there?
items.a: Put a spoonful of the salty water on a plate and let the water evaporate. White salt is left behind.
items.why: A strong answer names a way back and says what you would see. Evaporating is the best test, because it brings the salt back where everyone can see it.

items.p: Bread dries and browns when it is toasted. Which of these two changes goes back, and how do you know?
items.a: The drying goes back. Pale toasted squares went soft again in damp air. The browning does not go back: the colour scores stayed the same.
items.why: A strong answer separates the two changes and gives evidence for each one from a test.

items.p: Explain why a drop of ink never gathers itself again in a glass of water.
items.a: The ink particles move about at random. There are vastly more mixed arrangements than gathered ones, so the particles almost never come together again.
items.why: A strong answer compares the number of mixed arrangements with the number of sorted ones. It does not say that a new substance was made.

items.p: A city must choose which cups its tea stalls will use.

views.says: Use clay cups. A broken clay cup crumbles into harmless bits in the soil. But firing clay has no way back, so each cup is made once and used once.
Use steel. A steel tumbler is washed and used thousands of times. When it wears out, it is melted and made again. But washing needs water and soap.
Use paper cups. They are light and cheap. But each one has a thin plastic lining, so most cannot be made into paper again.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason that uses what you know about changes that go back. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason from the unit. One reason is that melting steel is reversible, so steel can be used without end. Another is that a fired clay cup can never be clay again.
items.why: Each view has something right in it. A strong answer says which changes go back and which do not. It takes the costs of water, fuel and waste seriously.

items.p: A white powder is stirred into a liquid. The liquid is dried, and a different powder is left. What happened?
items.why: If the powder had only dissolved, drying would have brought the same powder back. A different powder means a chemical change took place.

items.p: Scientists gently unfolded a protein, and it folded back by itself. What does this show?
opts: Unfolding does not break the chain
Heat was used to fold it
The protein was a new substance
items.why: A broken chain could not fold into its old shape. The chain stayed whole, and its shape was lost and found again.

items.p: Which test best shows whether a colour change is reversible?
opts: Try a way back and compare
See how dark the colour is
items.why: How a change looks does not tell you whether it goes back. You have to try a way back and compare the result with what you started with.

items.p: Masons keep a new concrete roof wet for many days. Why?
opts: Cement needs water to react and harden
Water stops the roof from melting
items.why: Cement hardens by a chemical change with water. If the concrete dries too soon, the change stops early and the roof is weaker.

items.p: A change that makes a new substance can never be pushed backwards.
items.why: False. Charging a battery pushes its chemical change backwards. Blood picks up oxygen in the lungs and lets it go again in the muscles.

items.p: Cooking an egg breaks its protein chains into small bits.
items.why: False. Heat unfolds the chains and they join into a net. The chains themselves stay whole.

items.p: Match each change in food to what happens inside.
items.why: The first three are cooking changes with no way back. The last one is dissolving, which makes no new substance.

items.p: Egg white starts to set at 62 degrees Celsius. An egg is at 27. How many degrees must it warm?
items.why: 62 minus 27 is 35. The 62 is a rounded figure. Below about 62 degrees Celsius the proteins keep their folded shapes, and the egg white stays runny.

items.p: The change that browns toast, dosas and roasted peanuts is called the ____ reaction.
items.why: It is named after Louis-Camille Maillard, who described it in 1912. Sugars and parts of proteins react on a hot, dry surface.

items.p: Two glasses hold the same flour and water. One was heated yesterday. How could you tell which, without tasting?
items.a: Leave both to stand. In the glass that was never heated, the flour settles into a white layer. The heated one stays thick and has no layer.
items.why: A strong answer uses a property that differs: raw flour settles and dries to a powder, and cooked paste does neither.

items.p: Plan a fair test: does a soaked chana seed shrink back when dried? Say what you keep the same.
items.a: Measure a row of 10 dry seeds, soak them overnight, measure again, dry them for two days and measure again. Use the same seeds, the same ruler and the same way of lining them up.
items.why: A strong answer measures before soaking, after soaking and after drying. It keeps the seeds and the measuring the same each time.

items.p: Glass can be melted and remade without end. Paper can be recycled only a few times. Explain the difference.
items.a: Melting glass is reversible, and the glass is unchanged. Each time paper is pulped, its fibres break shorter, and that breaking does not go back.
items.why: A strong answer says that glass goes through a reversible change each time, and paper through an irreversible one.

items.p: Tearing paper and toasting bread both have no way back. Say one way in which they differ.
items.a: Tearing makes no new substance: every piece is still paper. Toasting makes new brown substances that the bread did not have.
items.why: A strong answer separates two questions: whether a change goes back, and whether a new substance was made.

items.p: People disagree about whether food is better cooked or raw.

views.says: Cooking kills harmful microbes. It also lets the body take in more of the starch and protein.
Heat destroys part of the vitamin C in vegetables. Fresh fruit, salads and sprouts keep it.
Rice and rajma must be cooked. Cucumber and guava are best raw. A good meal has both kinds.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from this unit. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. One reason is that heat denatures the harmful protein in rajma for good. Another is that the loss of vitamin C also has no way back.
items.why: Each speaker is right about something. A strong answer sees that cooking makes irreversible changes, and that some of them help and some cost.

items.p: Draw a flow chart of how paneer is made. Mark each step with a two-way arrow or a one-way arrow.
items.a: Cold milk, a two-way arrow, hot milk, a one-way arrow marked 'lemon juice', curds and whey, a one-way arrow marked 'strain and press', paneer.
items.why: A two-way arrow means the step goes back, and a one-way arrow means it does not. A strong chart shows that heating milk goes back and that adding acid does not. It marks the acid step as the first one with no way back.

quiz.p: Which of these changes goes back most easily?
opts: Ghee setting on a cold day
quiz.why: Set ghee melts again with a little warmth. Cooking, burning and souring all make new substances.

quiz.p: Sand is stirred into water. What is the way back?
opts: Let it settle, then pour off the water
quiz.why: Sand does not dissolve. It sinks, and the water can be poured off or strained through a cloth.

quiz.p: In a reversible change, what stays the same?
quiz.why: Shape, temperature and state may all change. What stays is the substance: water is still water, and wax is still wax.

quiz.p: Steam turns to drops on a cold lid. What are the drops made of?
quiz.why: Condensing is a change of state. The water particles that left the pot as vapour have gathered again as liquid water.

quiz.p: Which of these shows that a new substance has formed?
opts: A new colour and smell that stay
quiz.why: A new substance has new properties, and they stay when the heat is gone. Getting wet, changing shape or cooling can all be undone.

quiz.p: What does heat do to the starch grains in flour and water?
quiz.why: Hot water gets into the grains, and they swell to many times their size and burst. This is called gelatinising, and it thickens the water.

quiz.p: Why does egg white turn from runny to solid when it is heated?
opts: Proteins unfold and join into a net
quiz.why: Heat shakes the folded protein chains open. The open chains stick to each other and hold the water still.

quiz.p: A square of brown toast is left to cool. What happens to its colour?
quiz.why: The brown comes from new substances made by the Maillard reaction. Taking the heat away does not turn them back.

quiz.p: How can you find out whether a change is reversible?
opts: Try a way back and compare
quiz.why: Heat and speed are poor guides. Melting uses heat and goes back. You have to try a way back and compare with what you started with.

quiz.p: Wheat ground into atta is still wheat. Can the grinding be undone?
opts: No, the bits cannot be rejoined
quiz.why: No new substance was made, but nothing joins the powder into whole grains again. A physical change can be irreversible.

quiz.p: Why does a shuffled pack of cards almost never come back in order?
opts: Mixed orders far outnumber sorted ones
quiz.why: Each shuffle gives another order of the cards. Nearly all the possible orders are mixed ones, so the sorted order almost never comes up.

quiz.p: Why can an old steel tumbler be made into a new one?
opts: Melting steel is a reversible change
Rust turns into steel in the sun
quiz.why: Steel melts in a furnace and sets again as steel. Because this change goes back, steel can be used again and again.

applications: Recycling works best for materials whose melting is reversible. Glass, steel and aluminium are melted and shaped again and again.
Salt makers at Thoothukudi in Tamil Nadu and in Kutch in Gujarat let the sun evaporate salty water. Dissolving goes back, so the salt is left.
A rechargeable battery holds a chemical change that goes both ways. Using the battery runs it forwards, and charging runs it backwards.
Milk is pasteurised by heating it. The heat denatures the proteins of harmful microbes, and that change does not go back when the milk cools.
Builders use the setting of cement, which has no way back. It gives roofs, bridges and dams that stay hard in the rain.
Medicine bottles, water bottles and jam jars have seals that snap or pop once. The seal uses an irreversible change to show that the pack was opened.
Batik makers draw with wax, which can be melted off again, before they use dye, which stays for good.

open_questions.q: How does a protein chain find its folded shape so fast?
open_questions.why_open: A chain could fold in more ways than anyone can count, yet most fold correctly in less than a second. Computers can now predict the final shape of many proteins. How the chain gets there is still being worked out.

open_questions.q: When did our ancestors first cook their food?
open_questions.why_open: The oldest widely accepted traces of fire used by our ancestors are about 1 million years old. Some scientists think cooking began much earlier, and old fireplaces are very hard to find.

open_questions.q: Why did the universe begin in such an orderly state?
open_questions.why_open: Changes run one way because the world moves from more orderly arrangements to less orderly ones. That only works if things were very orderly to begin with. Nobody knows why they were.

open_questions.q: Can a strong plastic be made that goes back fully to its starting substances?
open_questions.why_open: Most plastics get weaker each time they are melted, and some cannot be melted at all. Chemists are testing new plastics that can be taken apart and made again. None is in wide use yet.

open_questions.q: Can old concrete be turned back into fresh cement?
open_questions.why_open: Making cement gives off a great deal of carbon dioxide. Engineers are testing ways to reheat the cement from old concrete so that it can react with water again. It is not yet known how well this works for large buildings.

maths.problem: In The Slip Shuffle, 3 dotted and 3 blank slips can lie in 20 different orders. Only 2 of those orders are sorted. If you shake and draw 40 times, about how many rows will be sorted?
maths.explain: 2 sorted orders out of 20 is the same as 1 out of 10. 40 divided by 10 is 4. Your real count may be a little more or less, because each try is a matter of chance.
maths.context: In The Slip Shuffle you shake dotted and blank paper slips in a tumbler and lay them in a row. You count how often the dots come out together at one end.
maths.why_maths: Counting the possible orders tells you how often to expect a sorted row, before you do a single shake.

maths.problem: With 5 dotted and 5 blank slips, only 1 row in 126 comes out sorted. One try takes 5 seconds. About how long would you shake before you saw one sorted row? Give the answer in minutes and seconds.
maths.explain: 126 tries at 5 seconds each is 126 times 5, which is 630 seconds. 600 seconds is 10 minutes, and 30 seconds are left over. With only four more slips, the wait grows from under a minute to over ten minutes.
maths.context: In The Slip Shuffle, 6 slips came out sorted about 1 time in 10. This problem asks what happens with 10 slips.
maths.why_maths: Turning a chance into a waiting time shows how quickly un-mixing becomes hopeless as the number of pieces grows.

maths.problem: Here are made-up results from Cold Stir, Hot Stir. One tablespoon of flour weighed 9 grams. After settling and drying, 8 grams of flour came back from glass A. What fraction came back? Where could the missing gram be?
maths.answer: Eight ninths came back. The missing gram stayed in the water that was poured off, or stuck to the glass and the plate.
maths.explain: 8 grams out of 9 grams is eight ninths. No flour was destroyed. The finest grains had not settled yet, so they went down the sink with the water.
maths.context: In Cold Stir, Hot Stir, flour stirred into cold water settles to the bottom of glass A. The water is poured off and the flour is dried.
maths.why_maths: A fraction shows how complete the way back was. Asking where the rest went shows that 'reversible' does not mean that nothing gets spilt.

maths.problem: Here are made-up colour scores from The Toast Ladder. At 0 minutes the score was 0. At 1 minute it was 0. At 2 minutes it was 1. At 4 minutes it was 3. At 6 minutes it was 4. Did the colour rise by the same amount each minute? What score would you expect at 3 minutes?
maths.answer: No. Nothing changed in the first minute, and the colour rose fastest between 2 and 4 minutes. At 3 minutes the score would be about 2.
maths.explain: From 0 to 1 minute the score rose by 0. From 2 to 4 minutes it rose by 2, which is 1 for each minute. Halfway between a score of 1 and a score of 3 is 2. The bread has to dry before it can brown, so the start is slow.
maths.context: In The Toast Ladder, squares of bread sit on a hot tawa for different times. Each gets a colour score from 0 for white to 4 for nearly black.
maths.why_maths: Looking at the size of each step shows that browning starts late and then speeds up.

maths.problem: Egg white starts to set at about 62 degrees Celsius. Tap water is at 28 degrees. A cup of hot tea is at 70 degrees. Boiling water is at 100 degrees. In which of these would egg white start to set? How many degrees above the setting point is boiling water?
maths.answer: In the hot tea and in the boiling water. Boiling water is 38 degrees above the setting point.
maths.explain: 70 and 100 are both more than 62, and 28 is less. 100 minus 62 is 38. The change does not need boiling. It needs the egg white to pass 62 degrees Celsius.
maths.context: Heat makes the proteins in egg white unfold and join, and the egg white turns solid. This starts at about 62 degrees Celsius.
maths.why_maths: Comparing each temperature with one fixed number shows that a change with no way back can have a starting line.

maths.problem: Here are made-up results from Soak, Dry, Sprout. A row of 10 dry chana was 8 centimetres long. After soaking it was 12 centimetres. After two days of drying it was 9 centimetres. What fraction of the swelling was undone?
maths.answer: Three quarters of the swelling was undone.
maths.explain: The row grew by 12 minus 8, which is 4 centimetres. It shrank back by 12 minus 9, which is 3 centimetres. 3 out of 4 is three quarters. The seeds were probably not fully dry yet.
maths.context: In Soak, Dry, Sprout you measure a row of 10 chana seeds when dry, after soaking, and after drying again.
maths.why_maths: Comparing how far the row shrank with how far it grew tells you how much of the change went back.

how_we_found_out.story: A hundred years ago, many chemists thought that heat destroyed a protein. A boiled egg white could not be made runny again. So they supposed that its proteins had been broken up or turned into something else. In Beijing, the biochemist Hsien Wu tested proteins for years. He did this work with the biochemist Daisy Yen Wu, who became his wife in the 1920s and wrote many of the papers with him. In 1931 he proposed a different idea. A protein is a long chain folded into an exact shape, he said. Heat does not break the chain. It only makes the chain lose its folds, and the loose chains then stick to each other. Few scientists noticed his paper. Around 1960 the American scientist Christian Anfinsen found a way to test the idea. He took a protein from a cow's pancreas and unfolded the protein with chemicals. The protein stopped working. Then he took the chemicals away. The chains folded back by themselves and worked again. A broken chain could never have done that. Anfinsen won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1972.
how_we_found_out.who: Hsien Wu and Daisy Yen Wu in Beijing, and Christian Anfinsen in the United States
how_we_found_out.when: Wu published his theory in 1931. Anfinsen did his folding tests in the late 1950s and early 1960s, and won the Nobel Prize in 1972.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That heating a protein breaks it up or destroys it. Wu proposed that the chain only loses its folded shape. Anfinsen showed that an unfolded protein can fold back and work again, which a broken chain could not do.
how_we_found_out.art: A laboratory bench from the 1930s with glass flasks and a notebook, and above it a drawing of a long thread folded into a ball, opened out, and folded again.

roots.context: In this unit you stirred flour into cold and hot water, and you toasted a ladder of bread squares. Here we ask what it means that some changes go back and some do not.

deep_truth.truth: In The Toast Ladder, every square of bread could still be toasted darker. No square could be made paler again. So with a change that goes only one way, too little can be fixed and too much cannot. That is why a careful cook heats in small steps and checks each time.
deep_truth.habit: We treat 'a bit too much' and 'a bit too little' as mistakes of the same size. With a change that has no way back, they are different kinds of mistake. After too little, the right amount can still be reached. After too much, it cannot.
deep_truth.evidence: In The Toast Ladder, the pale 1-minute square went back on the tawa. It caught up with the brown 4-minute square. The 6-minute square stayed dark after cooling and after a night in damp air. In Cold Stir, Hot Stir, the heated flour could not be made thin again either.

three.who_am_i: Many of the changes that made you do not go back. Every meal you have digested is one of them, and so is every centimetre you have grown. At the same time, changes that do go back keep you alive every minute. Your blood picks up oxygen and lets it go again.
three.what_is_life: A living being uses both kinds of change. A dry seed can soak, dry and wait again. Once they grow a root, they have chosen a change with no way back.
three.what_is_this_world: The world uses the same water again and again through changes that go back. But the world also has a past and a future, because some changes never go back.

roots.thread: Changes that go back let the world use one substance many times. The water in your glass has been cloud, rain and river before. Changes with no way back are how new things come to exist: toast, a pot, a grown tree, a star's helium. Everything is conscious, down to the particles. So each of these changes is something that happens to someone, and not only to a thing. Many sages taught that all things come from one source, which keeps making new things. The science of this unit adds one plain point. New things keep coming into being, and the change can be slowed down or steered, but it cannot be taken back.

teachings.teaching: Tiruvalluvar wrote that a crow can defeat an owl by day. In the same way, he said, a ruler who wants to win must choose the right time.
teachings.link: The Kural is about a ruler and an enemy, and it is not about toast. But the lesson fits in the same way. The same act can succeed at one time and fail at another. In The Toast Ladder, taking the bread off the tawa worked only before it turned too dark.

teachings.teaching: The Buddha taught that all things that are put together are impermanent. A person who sees this clearly, he said, turns away from suffering.
teachings.link: The verse says that nothing made stays as it is. This unit agrees and adds a detail. Some things change and come back, as water does. Others change once, as toast does.

teachings.source: Heraclitus, as quoted by Plato in the Cratylus, 402a
teachings.teaching: The Greek thinker Heraclitus said that you cannot step twice into the same river. New water is always flowing in.
teachings.link: A river looks the same from day to day, yet its water is always new. Even changes that 'go back' do not return the world to exactly what it was. The ghee that sets again has lost a little heat to the room.

science.text: A protein that has lost its shape still has a whole chain. Some proteins fold back by themselves when the cause is taken away. Christian Anfinsen showed this around 1960.
Nobody knows why the universe began in a state so orderly that changes have run one way ever since.

other_view.view: They point out that no atom is lost in any change. So in principle, with enough energy and skill, toast could be taken apart and built into bread again. On this view nothing is truly irreversible. 'No way back' only describes the tools we have today. Many of them also say that bread and wax are not aware of anything.

practice.title: The pause before the tear
practice.say: Hold a small piece of scrap paper in both hands, ready to tear it. Stop there. Breathe in and out slowly three times. Right now the paper is still whole, and you could still choose to keep it whole. Now tear it slowly and listen. Hold the two pieces. The whole paper is gone, and only the torn paper is left.
practice.kid: Hold a paper, ready to tear. Stop. Breathe slowly three times. Now tear it slowly. Listen. Look at the two pieces.

ask: A cooked egg holds almost every atom the raw egg held. What exactly cannot be got back?
Before you tore the paper, you could still choose to keep it whole. After you tore it, the whole paper was gone. Where did the whole paper go?
The Sun turns hydrogen into helium and cannot turn it back. Is the Sun running down, or is it making something?

playtest: Read through as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, step by step. The experiments were reasoned through and have not yet been tried at home. Cold Stir, Hot Stir (core) needs cornflour, rice flour or maida, two clear glasses and a stove for about 4 minutes. With cornflour, the cold glass usually shows a white layer about 5 millimetres thick within 10 to 30 minutes. The heated mix sets into a soft paste with no layer. With rice flour or maida the water above the layer stays a little milky. Atta leaves brown bran. So cornflour is the best choice. The plates must be spread thin. In dry weather they dry in a few hours. In the monsoon they can take a day and a half. If plate B is still sticky, wait longer. The Toast Ladder (core) needs two slices of bread, a tawa and a steel box. Tawas and flames differ. If the 2-minute square is already dark, the step tells the grown-up to lower the flame and start again. After a night in damp air the pale squares are usually soft and the dark ones bendy. No colour changes. In very dry weather, wet the cloth with 3 teaspoons of water. Nobody eats the squares from the damp box. Five Changes, Three Piles uses cold milk, which makes fine lumps with lemon juice in about a minute. Warm milk makes bigger lumps. The Slip Shuffle depends on chance. A family's tally may differ from the expected 4 in 12 and 2 in 20. The parent notes say so. Soak, Dry, Sprout needs four days. Chana usually sprout in one to two days at 25 to 30 degrees Celsius. They are slower in a cool room. The dried seeds come back close to their first size, and not exactly to it. Tangled Threads, the two card games and The Tell-Tale Seal need only wool, paper, glue and coins. No part needs a garden. The stove is used by a grown-up in Cold Stir, Hot Stir and The Toast Ladder.
